title: Final: Jobs and Burst basics
sub: Threads and the compiler, HPC#, kinds of jobs and a frame with Schedule and Complete — no hints
cards/0/q: Say it out loud: “How is the Job System different from Burst?” Which answer would you give?
cards/0/options/0: They are two independent things. The Job System spreads work over worker threads, respects dependencies and catches races in the Editor. Burst is a compiler: HPC# through LLVM into native code with SIMD. Together you get parallel code that is fast on every thread, and Burst also works without jobs, on a static method
cards/0/options/1: Burst is a newer version of the Job System with multithreading support
cards/0/options/2: The Job System exists so that Burst can work: without jobs Burst is not used
cards/0/options/3: They are the same thing: Burst is an attribute that turns on worker threads
cards/0/explain: A strong answer separates the axes: threads versus machine code. Plus two signs of experience — the four combinations (Burst without jobs exists) and “profile first”.
cards/0/wrong/1: Burst is a compiler, not a scheduler. It creates no threads.
cards/0/wrong/2: Burst also compiles static methods called from the main thread, and Run() with no worker threads.
cards/0/wrong/3: Worker threads come from Schedule(); [BurstCompile] only changes what code Execute runs as.
cards/1/q: Which of these will Burst not compile? Pick all that apply.
cards/1/options/0: A string title field in a job struct
cards/1/options/1: A local List<int> variable inside Execute
cards/1/options/4: A Func<int, int> field in a job struct
cards/1/explain: A string, a List and a delegate are managed objects, and HPC# has none. Unity.Mathematics, FixedString and native containers are exactly the Burst-friendly replacements.
cards/2/q: Match the task with the job type.
cards/2/pairs/3/0: The same code, sometimes on the main thread for debugging, sometimes in parallel
cards/2/pairs/4/0: Visit every entity with LocalTransform and Speed components
cards/3/q: Which line throws a safety-system exception in the Editor?
cards/3/explain: The job that writes positions is still running while the main thread already reads positions[0]. In the Editor the safety system stops this with an exception; in a build you would read a half-written element. Read it in LateUpdate after Complete().
cards/4/q: Trap: an IJobFor is started with job.Schedule(n, default). The profiler shows all the work on one worker thread. Why?
cards/4/options/0: Schedule on an IJobFor runs all iterations in order on one worker thread; ScheduleParallel is the parallel one
cards/4/options/3: IJobFor cannot run in parallel at all
cards/4/explain: IJobFor has three modes: Run — the main thread, Schedule — one worker thread, ScheduleParallel — batches on several. The job type is the same; the call picks the mode.
cards/4/wrong/1: Burst changes the code, not the number of threads.
cards/4/wrong/2: Schedule on an IJobFor has no batchSize at all.
cards/5/q: An input check in a Burst job must give a clear error in the Editor and must not crash the player build. How do you do it?
cards/5/options/0: Put the throw in a method marked [Conditional("ENABLE_UNITY_COLLECTIONS_CHECKS")] and call it from Execute
cards/5/options/2: Leave the throw in Execute: in a build safety checks switch it off
cards/5/options/3: Call Debug.LogError instead of throw and carry on
cards/5/explain: In the Editor the symbol is defined, so the check runs and throws. In a player build the method and its calls disappear. An ordinary throw from Burst code in a player build is an abort.
cards/5/wrong/2: Safety checks are unavailable in player builds, and an ordinary throw stays there and aborts the app.
cards/5/wrong/3: You can log, but then the code goes on with bad data — that is a warning, not a check.
cards/6/q: A static method with [BurstCompile] is called from the main thread. What did you get?
cards/6/options/0: Native Burst code on the same main thread — no parallelism, but faster than managed code
cards/6/options/1: Work on the worker threads, like a job
cards/6/options/2: Nothing: Burst only works inside jobs
cards/6/explain: That is combination 3: Burst without worker threads. The declaring type must be marked [BurstCompile] too, the method is not generic, structs go by ref, in or pointer, and it pays to hand such a call a whole batch of work.
cards/6/wrong/1: Only the Job System gives you threads; a direct call runs where it was made.
cards/6/wrong/3: A direct call is an ordinary method call, with no queue.
cards/7/task: Write HealJob : IJobFor with [BurstCompile]: fields hp (NativeArray<float>), regen ([ReadOnly] NativeArray<float>), float dt and float maxHp. Execute(int i) adds regen[i] * dt to hp[i] and caps the result with math.min(…, maxHp). In Healing.Schedule create the job and return the handle from ScheduleParallel(hp.Length, 64, dependsOn).
cards/7/checks/0/label: HealJob is an IJobFor struct with [BurstCompile]
cards/7/checks/2/label: Execute(int i) writes hp[i] using math.min
cards/7/checks/3/label: There is no for loop in Execute
cards/7/checks/5/label: The method does not return dependsOn instead of the job’s handle
cards/7/explain: One iteration is one element, with no loop and no foreign indices, so the job splits into batches safely. ScheduleParallel hands batches of 64 to the worker threads, and the caller passes the returned handle on as a dependency or waits on it with Complete(). Return dependsOn and nobody ever waits for HealJob itself.
cards/8/task: Finish Mover: VelocityJob : IJobParallelForTransform with [BurstCompile] moves transform.position by velocity[index] * dt (velocity is a [ReadOnly] NativeArray<Vector3>, dt is a float). In Update schedule the job over the transforms field and wake the workers right away; call Complete() in LateUpdate.
cards/8/checks/0/label: VelocityJob is an IJobParallelForTransform struct with [BurstCompile]
cards/8/checks/5/label: There is no Complete() in Update
cards/8/explain: The transforms move on worker threads while the rest of the frame’s Update calls run, and LateUpdate collects the finished work. ScheduleBatchedJobs keeps the job from sitting in the local queue until Complete(). And remember the hierarchy: under a shared root the read-write Schedule runs everything on one thread.
cards/9/q: Build the answer to “How would you speed up a hot loop?”
cards/9/items/0: Find the hot spot in the profiler
cards/9/items/1: Move the data into native containers and structs
cards/9/items/2: Move the loop body into an IJobFor and mark it [BurstCompile]
cards/9/items/3: ScheduleParallel in Update, Complete() in LateUpdate
cards/9/items/4: Measure again: the profiler Timeline and the Burst Inspector
cards/9/explain: Measure — data — a Burst job — schedule early, complete late — measure again. That sequence is the answer that tells the interviewer you have done it yourself.
cards/10/body:
A 30–60 minute task. Unity 6 with the Burst, Collections and Mathematics packages. One component moves 200,000 points every frame: NativeArray<float3> positions and velocities, allocated in Awake with Allocator.Persistent and freed in OnDestroy.

Steps.
1. A loop in Update on the main thread — note the Update time in the Profiler.
2. The same loop in an IJob without Burst: Schedule() and right away Complete().
3. Add [BurstCompile]. In the Editor turn on Jobs > Burst > Synchronous Compilation, or the first frames run without Burst.
4. Switch to IJobFor and ScheduleParallel(Count, 64, default).
5. Spread it across the frame: Schedule and JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() in Update, Complete() in LateUpdate.

What to measure. In the Profiler (CPU Usage, Timeline view): main-thread and worker-thread time for every step, and in LateUpdate how long Complete() waits (the WaitForJobGroupID marker). In the Burst Inspector (Jobs > Burst > Open Inspector) find your job, turn on “Highlight SIMD Scalar vs Packed” and check which instructions the hot loop uses: packed (vmulps, vaddps) or scalar (vmulss, vaddss). Why an array of float3 vectorizes worse than separate float arrays is covered in unit 3.

How you know it worked. Step 3 is clearly faster than step 2 on the same single thread — that is Burst’s share; in step 4 the work shows up as bars on several worker threads; in step 5 the main thread barely waits in LateUpdate; the console shows no leak warnings. Take the final numbers in a Development build with the profiler attached, because the Editor runs safety checks. Write down a “step → ms” table — that is a ready-made story for the interview.
